sensitivity_note: No SPEC Section 6 subject-matter sensitivity applies -- this is a business/marketing decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: The Broadcast Blitz projects roughly 330 paying subscribers against the $60,000 budget (about $182 cost per acquisition) versus Plan B's roughly 287 subscribers (about $209 cost per acquisition) -- Plan A wins by about 15%, and it wins on sheer channel reach: two TV packages plus radio put FlowState in front of far more total people than SEO and a single magazine placement ever could, even though each of those impressions converts at a much lower rate.
balance.argument_b: The Precision Funnel spends most of its budget on the two channels with the highest per-visitor conversion rates in the entire case (SEO's real 6.8% Google Ads conversion rate is nearly 6x the 1.17% rate every broadcast/print channel gets), and it is far less exposed to the two Modeling Assumptions the case is most sensitive to (TV CPM and TV awareness rate) -- a plausible seasonal swing in TV pricing barely touches Plan B's economics and now more than erodes Plan A's lead (see sensitivity/twist below).
balance.margin_basis: Sum, for each plan, the projected paying subscribers across all five channels and both segments (reach x segment share x awareness x interest x trial-conversion x adoption, per case.md Appendix D's rates), then compare the two plans' totals as a percent difference.
balance.twist_effect: REVISED 2026-09-11 (Appendix A channel-cost sourcing pass): MA3 (TV -- General broadcast CPM) was retuned from $24.00 to $30.00 after a tighter, broadcast-specific real source [S14] was found, which raises Plan A's exposure to a TV-pricing swing. A +50% seasonal premium on both TV packages' CPM (trade-show week overlapping championship-season live-sports inventory) now takes Plan A to about 259.82 and Plan B to about 263.16 -- Plan B pulls ahead by about 1.3%, actually flipping the winner at exactly the disclosed +50% premium (previously the same +50% premium only narrowed the margin to 1.8% without flipping it; the crossover point itself moved from roughly +57% to roughly +44.8% CPM premium). Disclosed here, never in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's student-facing sections.
balance.stability: Base margin (15.1%) is a direct function of MA2/MA3 (TV CPM point-values) and MA5-MA8 (segment skew, awareness, interest). The system-of-equations break-even point (D4) is a separate, correct, computable quantity for the student to find -- it is not disclosed here as a spoiler beyond the mechanics needed to grade it. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the parameters most likely to change the verdict.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2 picks a specific point-value ($14) from a real but wide, undifferentiated cable CPM range ($10-$30, S2) that does not separately break out a sports/fitness-network rate -- a documented good-faith estimate from the closest public analogue, not a directly quoted sports-specific figure. Flexing this -50% breaches the SPEC section 2 20% cap (margin 40.6%). A facilitator should treat MA2 as one of the two most load-bearing assumptions in the model.

MA3 (revised 2026-09-11) picks a specific point-value ($30) from a narrower, broadcast-specific real range ($25-$40, S14) -- a documented estimate within a sourced range, not a directly quoted figure for this exact campaign. This is the single most load-bearing assumption in the model: flexing it -50% breaches the 20% cap (margin 29.6%), and a joint +50% swing on MA2+MA3 together (the disclosed FACILITATOR.md twist) flips the winner outright, Plan B edging ahead by about 1.3%.

MA4's own basis states no public source publishes an exact drive-time radio CPM; the case's $10.00 was kept only as a plausibility cross-check against a real weekly-package cost (S3) and a real blended average (S16), not a directly quoted drive-time figure. This is a genuine forecast/irreducible-unknown dial, not a modeling error. Flexing -50% breaches the SPEC section 2 20% cap (margin 23.7%); no retune was applied because $10.00 is already a real, disclosed, non-extreme choice, and narrowing it further would misrepresent how uncertain drive-time radio pricing actually is.

MA6 sets a brand-new, previously-unadvertised product's TV awareness rate with no directly comparable published benchmark (informed only by a general TV-vs-digital lift figure, S8). This is an irreducible forecast quantity for a product and campaign that do not yet exist. Flexing -50% actually flips the winner (B overtakes A) -- a distinct instability from FACILITATOR.md's scripted twist (a +50% premium on MA2/MA3's TV CPMs), not the same mechanism -- confirming this case's margin is fragile to more than one lever, not only the trade-show CPM story. Not an undiscovered defect; a facilitator should expect a sharp student to challenge this assumption directly.

MA8 sets the aware-to-website-visit rate for TV with no public source measuring this for a specific new product; it is set as a modest, generic fraction of the prior funnel stage. Flexing -50% flips the winner (B overtakes A), the same disclosed instability as tv_awareness above, since both scale the same TV funnel stage. The case's entire premise -- that a broad-reach plan and a narrow-high-intent plan can be genuinely close -- depends on this assumption pointing in the direction stated.

facilitator.twist: A seasonal TV-rate premium (trade-show week overlapping championship-season live-sports programming) raises both TV packages' CPM by about 50%, flipping the winner -- Plan B edges ahead of Plan A by about 1.3%.
